Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Money, work & business · Work & responsibility

competition noun

rivalry, competing

also rivalry, the competition, competitors, compete, competitive

classical

Tac. Agr. 21.1: honōris aemulātiō
Levi–Bini p. 17

aemulātiō, aemulātiōnis f.

noun, third declension

rivalry, the effort to equal or outdo others

In a good or a bad sense, as Cicero says (Tusc. 4.17); jealous rivalry is rīvālitās (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • ita honōris aemulātiō prō necessitāte erat

    so competition for praise did the work of compulsionTac. Agr. 21.1

  • sunt etiam nōnnūllī acuendīs puerōrum ingeniīs nōn inūtilēs lūsūs, cum positīs invicem cujusque generis quaestiunculīs aemulantur

    some games are also useful for sharpening children’s wits, when they compete by setting each other little questions of every kindQuint. 1.3.11

Other words

  • contentiō, contentiōnis f. — a contest, a struggle; competition

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.87: ambitiō honōrumque contentiō, the competition for office; Traupman 44; Levi–Bini p. 17

  • aemulor, aemulārī, aemulātus sum — compete with, try to outdo

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Quint. 1.3.11

See also competition, business.

SourcesLewis & Short: aemulatio · Lewis & Short: contentio · Lewis & Short: aemulor

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 44, checked against the searchable text of the book (9 November 2026).

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-tacitus, loci-quintilianus), checked against the editions named there.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
